en: The Questions of Milinda:
The Chapter on the Puzzles, Section on the Power of Supernormal Faculties (Iddhibalavagga)

8. The Question on the Severing of Unwholesomeness “Venerable Nāgasena, did the Tathāgata attain omniscience after having incinerated all unwholesome states, or did he attain omniscience while some unwholesome states still remained?
“Great King, the Blessed One attained omniscience after having incinerated all unwholesome states; there is no remainder of unwholesomeness in the Blessed One.”
“But, venerable sir, have painful feelings ever arisen in the body of the Tathāgata before?
“Yes, great king. At Rājagaha, the Blessed One’s foot was wounded by a splinter; he suffered from the disease of blood-and-bile;
when his body was congested, a purgative was administered by Jīvaka; and when a wind-disorder arose, it was attended to by the Elder attendant.”
“...and sought out hot water.

[The opponent says: “Venerable Nāgasena, if the Tathāgata attained omniscience after burning away all unwholesome states, then that statement—that the Blessed One’s foot was wounded by a splinter and the disease of bloody flux arose—is false.”

“If it is true that the Tathāgata’s foot was wounded by a splinter and the disease of blood-flowing sores arose, then the statement that the Tathāgata, having burnt away all unwholesome states, attained omniscience is also false.

Venerable sir, there is no experiencing of feeling without karma; all that experiencing of feeling is rooted in karma, and one experiences it precisely because of karma. This too is a dilemma involving two sides that has come to you, and it must be resolved by you.
“No, Great King, not all that experiencing of feeling is rooted in karma.”
"By eight causes, Great King, do feelings arise, by which various beings experience sensations.
What are the eight?
Great King, here certain feelings arise originating from wind."
“Furthermore, Great King, those diseases arising from bile …pe… those arising from phlegm …pe… and those arising from a combination of the humors …pe…”

“Furthermore, Great King, there are those born from a change in the seasons …pe… there are those born from an irregular lifestyle …pe… there are those born from self-inflicted injury, Great King …pe…”
“Furthermore, Great King, certain feelings born of the ripening of kamma arise here.
It is by these eight causes, Great King, that various beings experience feelings.
In this regard, those persons who would say, ‘Kamma afflicts beings,’ are rejecting these seven causes.”
“That statement of theirs is false. “Venerable Nāgasena, that which is caused by wind,
that which is caused by bile, that which is caused by phlegm, that which is caused by a combination of these, that which arises from changes in the seasons,
that which arises from improper conduct, and that which arises from external violence— all of these are indeed originated by karma alone.”
“All these arise through karma alone.
“If, Great King, all those ailments were indeed produced solely by karma, they would not have distinct characteristics according to their categories.

For wind, Great King, when it becomes deranged, does so in ten ways: by cold, by heat, by hunger, by thirst, by overeating, by standing, by exertion, by running about, by external assault, and by the ripening of karma.”
In that regard, those nine types [of feelings] do not arise in the past, nor in the future, but arise in the present existence; therefore, it cannot be said that “all feeling originates from karma.
Great King, when bile becomes disturbed, it is disturbed in three ways: by cold, by heat, and by irregular food.
Great King, when phlegm becomes disturbed, it is disturbed in three ways: by cold, by heat, and by food and drink.
And as for the wind, O Great King, and the bile, and the phlegm—when they become disturbed by their respective provocations and become mixed together, each draws forth its own specific sensation.
Sensation born from a change in the seasons, O Great King, arises through a change in the seasons;
sensation born from an irregularity in conduct arises through an irregularity in conduct.

“Great King, there are feelings born of exertion that are functional (kiriyā), and there are feelings that are the result of kamma (kammavipāka). A feeling born of the result of kamma arises through kamma performed in the past.
Thus, Great King, that which is born of the result of kamma is little, while the remainder is much more.
Regarding this, fools overreach by thinking, ‘Everything is indeed born of the result of kamma.’”
That karma cannot be defined without the knowledge of a Buddha.
Furthermore, Great King, as for that sensation when the Blessed One’s foot was wounded by a splinter,
it was not born of wind, nor born of bile, nor born of phlegm, nor born of a combination of these, nor born of a change in the seasons.
It arises from an uneven avoidance [of danger], not from the ripening of karma; it is purely due to an external assault.
For, Great King, throughout many hundreds of thousands of births, Devadatta harbored malice toward the Tathāgata.
Because of that malice, he seized a large, heavy rock and released it, thinking, "I shall drop it upon his head. Then, two other rocks...
Having approached, they caught that rock even before the Tathāgata had reached it;
by their impact, the rock split apart and fell upon the Blessed One’s foot, drawing blood.
Whether, O Great King, this pain of the Blessed One arose from the ripening of karma (*kamma-vipāka*) or from a mere action (*kiriyā*), there is no other kind of feeling beyond these.
Just as, Great King, a seed does not germinate because of a defect in the field or because of a defect in the seed;
even so, Great King, this feeling of the Blessed One has arisen either from the ripening of karma or from a mere functional act (kiriyā), and beyond that there is no other feeling.
Or again, Great King, just as food is digested improperly because of a defect in the stomach or because of a defect in the food.
In the same way, Great King, this feeling of the Blessed One has arisen either from the ripening of karma or from a functional act; beyond that, there is no other feeling.
Moreover, Great King, the Blessed One has no feeling born of the ripening of karma, nor does he have any feeling born of the avoidance of uneven ground;
the Blessed One’s feelings arise through the remaining modes of origination, and by means of those feelings—
"It is not possible to deprive the Blessed One of life.
Great King, desirable and undesirable, pleasant and unpleasant feelings fall upon this body composed of the four great elements.

Great King, suppose a clod of earth were thrown into the air; it would fall upon the great earth. Would that clod of earth, Great King, fall upon the great earth because of anything done in the past?"
“No indeed, venerable sir. There is no cause, venerable sir, by which the great earth could experience the result of wholesome or unwholesome kamma;
rather, venerable sir, that clod of earth falls upon the great earth due to a present, effortless cause.
“Great king, just as the great earth is, so should the Tathāgata be regarded.”
"Just as a clod of earth falls upon the great earth because it was not made beforehand,
even so, Great King, that splinter fell upon the foot of the Tathāgata because it was not made beforehand.
But here, Great King, when people break and dig into the great earth, do those people break and dig into the great earth because it was made beforehand?"
“No indeed, Bhante.
“In the same way, Great King, as for that splinter which fell upon the Blessed One’s foot, that splinter did not fall upon the Blessed One’s foot because of anything done in the past.
And even that affliction from which the Blessed One suffered—the discharge of blood—that affliction too was not caused by anything done in the past.”
Whatever bodily ailments arose in the Blessed One, Great King, they did not arise from the ripening of kamma;
rather, they were produced from one or another of these six origins.
This was spoken, Great King, by the Blessed One, the God beyond Gods, in the *Moliyasīvaka* discourse within the *Saṃyutta Nikāya*, the most excellent seal:
“Sīvaka, here certain feelings arise originating from bile.
This, Sīvaka, is to be known by oneself: that here certain feelings arise originating from bile.
This, Sīvaka, is also recognized as true by the world: that here certain feelings arise originating from bile.”

In this regard, Sīvaka, those ascetics and brahmins who hold such a doctrine and such a view as: "Whatever this person experiences—whether pleasure, pain, or neither-pleasure-nor-pain—all that is caused by what was done in the past"—they overstep both what they have known for themselves and what is generally accepted as truth in the world.
Therefore, I say that the views of those ascetics and brahmins are wrong.
“Sīvaka, here too certain feelings arise originating from bile; certain feelings arise originating from wind;
and certain feelings arise from a combination [of the humors], Sīvaka.”
“Sīvaka, there are also [diseases] born of a change in the seasons...
Sīvaka, there are also those born from the improper handling of food...
Sīvaka, there are also those resulting from self-inflicted injury...”
"Sīvaka, here certain feelings born of the ripening of kamma arise.
This, Sīvaka, should be known by oneself: that here certain feelings born of the ripening of kamma arise.
This, Sīvaka, is also recognized as true by the world: that here certain feelings born of the ripening of kamma arise."

“In this regard, Sīvaka, as for those ascetics and brahmins who speak thus and hold such a view: ‘Whatever this person experiences—whether pleasure, pain, or neither-pain-nor-pleasure—all that is caused by what was done in the past’—they overstep what they have known for themselves, and they overstep what is considered true in the world.
Therefore, I say that the views of those ascetics and brahmins are wrong.”

“Thus, Great King, not all feeling is born as the result of karma; rather, Great King, it is because he has burned away all unwholesomeness that the Blessed One attained omniscience—bear this in mind thus.
“It is well, venerable Nāgasena; it is so, and I accept it as such.
This is the eighth dilemma: The Severing of Unwholesomeness.
